items.title: The Khalsa was founded at Vaisakhi 1699
items.claim: What did Guru Gobind Singh establish in 1699?

options.text: A new Sikh state in northern India
The Khalsa (the 'pure') — a community of initiated Sikhs marked by the Five Ks (Kesh, Kara, Kanga, Kachera, Kirpan), open to all castes and gender
A revised version of the Guru Granth Sahib
A peace treaty with the Mughal Empire

items.reveal:
At Anandpur on Vaisakhi (April) 1699, Guru Gobind Singh called for volunteers willing to die for the faith. The Panj Pyare (Five Beloved Ones) came forward, were initiated with amrit (sweetened water stirred with a double-edged sword), and were then themselves used to initiate Gobind Singh.

The Five Ks: Kesh (uncut hair, including the dastaar turban), Kara (steel bracelet), Kanga (wooden comb), Kachera (cotton undergarment), Kirpan (small sword).

The Khalsa took the surname Singh (lion) for men and Kaur (princess) for women — symbolically equalising caste and gender.
items.why: Sikh identity has visible bodily markers that emerged from a specific 1699 event with named participants. The Five Ks are not vague cultural symbols but coded responses to Mughal-era persecution and caste hierarchy.

items.title: Kosher rules separate meat and dairy
items.claim: What are the main categories of kosher (kashrut) restrictions?

options.text: Permitted animals (mammals that chew cud and have cloven hooves; fish with fins and scales); ritual slaughter (shechita); separation of meat and dairy in cooking, eating and utensils; specific prohibitions including pork, shellfish, mixing milk and meat
Only meals at synagogue must be kosher

items.reveal:
The meat-dairy separation derives from three repetitions of 'You shall not boil a kid in its mother's milk' (Exodus 23:19, 34:26; Deuteronomy 14:21). Rabbinic interpretation extended this to all mixing of meat and dairy.

Leviticus 11 and Deuteronomy 14 list permitted and forbidden animals. Pork and shellfish are the most widely known prohibitions; rabbit, camel and birds of prey are also forbidden.

Shechita is ritual slaughter by a trained shochet with a perfectly sharp knife in a single cut — designed to be quick and to drain blood. Some European countries (Sweden, Norway, Switzerland, Belgian regions) have banned shechita without prior stunning on animal welfare grounds.
items.why: Religious practice is often embodied — daily eating, household kitchens, separate dishes. Kashrut is one of the clearest cases of belief expressed through bodily and domestic practice.

items.title: The Sunni-Shia split began as a political dispute about succession
items.claim: What is the origin of the Sunni-Shia division?

options.text: Two communities formed in different countries centuries apart

After Muhammad's death in 632 CE, the question of succession divided those who supported Abu Bakr (Sunni) from those who held Ali, Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law, had been designated (Shia) — fully entrenched after the martyrdom of Husayn at Karbala in 680 CE
A modern political invention with no early roots

items.reveal:
Muhammad died on 8 June 632 without naming a successor unambiguously. Abu Bakr was chosen as the first caliph; Ali became fourth caliph (656-661) after the assassinations of Umar and Uthman.

The First Fitna (civil war) and Husayn ibn Ali's death at Karbala on 10 Muharram 61 AH (10 October 680 CE) crystallised Shia identity. The annual commemoration of Ashura mourns Husayn.

Today: around 85-90% of Muslims are Sunni, 10-15% Shia. Shia majorities: Iran, Iraq, Azerbaijan, Bahrain. Significant minorities: Lebanon, Yemen, Syria, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Afghanistan, India.
items.why: Religious traditions can be deeply shaped by political beginnings. The Sunni-Shia distinction is real and consequential — and originally a question about who should lead, not what to believe.
